title: Buffer solution
sentences: A buffer solution is a solution whose pH does not change significantly on dilution or if a small amount of strong acid or base is added to it at constant temperature.
Buffer capacity is used to measure the resistance to pH change of a buffer solution.
Buffer solutions are used to maintain pH at a nearly constant value in a wide variety of chemical applications.
In nature, many living systems use buffering to regulate pH.
For example, the bicarbonate buffering system serves to regulate the pH of blood, and bicarbonate also acts as a buffer in the ocean.
Once the acid is more than 95% deprotonated, the pH rises rapidly because most of the added alkali is consumed in the neutralization reaction.

The buffer capacity (β) is a measure of the amount (number of moles or gram-equivalents, Δ n) of a strong acid or base added to a given volume (V) of solution required to change its pH by a given amount (Δ p H).
The buffer capacity (β) is highest when the addition of a large amount (Δ n) of acid or base to the solution volume produces only a small pH change (Δ p H).
Thus buffer capacity and the closely related buffer index are quantitative measures of a buffer solution's resistance to changes in pH in response to changes in acid or alkali concentration.
Buffer capacity and buffer index are quasi-synonyms (both are denoted β), but their definitions differ slightly in the extent of pH change they consider.

The concept of buffer capacity, how to determine it from acid-base titration measurements, and its mathematical significance in relation to the dissociation constant (p Kₐ) of the buffer solution and its behaviour in response to an external perturbation were introduced by the Dutch-American biochemist Donald Dexter Van Slyke in 1922.

The buffer index (also β) considers an infinitesimal change in pH (for mathematical calculation purposes), whereas the buffer capacity considers a macroscopic pH change of 1 pH unit (for titration measurements).

The equilibrium concentrations of these three components can be calculated in an ICE table (ICE standing for "initial, change, equilibrium").

The first row, labelled I, lists the initial conditions: the concentration of acid is C₀, initially undissociated, so the concentrations of A⁻ and H⁺ would be zero; y is the initial concentration of added strong acid, such as hydrochloric acid.
If strong alkali, such as sodium hydroxide, is added, then y will have a negative sign because alkali removes hydrogen ions from the solution.
The second row, labelled C for "change", specifies the changes that occur when the acid dissociates.
The acid concentration decreases by an amount −x, and the concentrations of A⁻ and H⁺ both increase by an amount +x.
This follows from the equilibrium expression.
The third row, labelled E for "equilibrium", adds together the first two rows and shows the concentrations at equilibrium.
To find x, use the formula for the equilibrium constant in terms of concentrations: Kₐ = ([ H⁺ ] [ A⁻ ])/([ HA ]).
Substitute the concentrations with the values found in the last row of the ICE table: Kₐ = (x (x + y))/(C₀ − x).
With specific values for C₀, Kₐ and y, this equation can be solved for x.
Assuming that pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], the pH can be calculated as pH = −log₁₀(x + y).
